title: Inquest set for March 3 in 2012 death at Duncan RCMP cells
subtitle: There will be a public inquest into the death of a 34-year-old man in North Cowichan/Duncan RCMP cells. Jeremy David Richardson was taken to police cells around 11 a.m.
article: There will be a public inquest into the death of a 34-year-old man in North Cowichan/Duncan RCMP cells.

Jeremy David Richardson was taken to police cells around 11 a.m. on April 21, 2012, after he was found drunk and passed out in a public area of downtown Duncan. He had declined assistance from B.C. Ambulance paramedics but police took him in to sober up.
Three hours later, Richardson was found to be in medical distress by a guard.
He was taken by ambulance to Cowichan District Hospital and then airlifted to Victoria's Royal Jubilee Hospital. He died at noon the next day.
The inquest will begin March 3 at the courthouse in Duncan, the B.C. Coroners Service announced Monday.
Regional coroner Matthew Brown and a jury will hear evidence from witnesses to determine the facts surrounding the death.
A coroner's inquest doesn't determine wrongdoing but may lead to recommendations aimed at preventing future deaths under similar circumstances.

The Oak Bay police investigated and ruled out any wrongdoing or use of force by North Cowichan/Duncan RCMP staff. Investigators reviewed video from the cell and interviewed officers involved as well as people who saw Richardson before his arrest.
North Cowichan/Duncan detachment commander Sgt. Jack McNeil said he's satisfied his officers acted appropriately and arrested Richardson without using force.

"Policy had been complied with and there were no events or incidents that caused us concern about any of the officers in the performance of their duties," McNeil said. "We were quite pleased with how promptly the guard on duty recognized he was having some distressed breathing."
Richardson was well known to police and struggled with addiction, McNeil said. Toxicology results showed the cause of death was a lethal mix of alcohol and drugs.

"I welcome an inquest just to really allow the public to see how these things can transpire and, hopefully, confirm public trust in how police deal with people who are poly-substance abusers," McNeil said.
